title.en: If you had only three days

text.en: Think of a place you loved visiting. What did you see there? What did you hear and smell? Now imagine that you could not see or hear. Our five senses help us experience and make sense of the world. In this essay, Helen Keller, who was both blind and deaf, tells us what she would see if she were given sight for just three days.

You recall a visit to a place you liked, write its name, who you went with, and what you could see, then think how it would feel and be different if you could not see or hear.
Helen Keller finds hundreds of things to interest her through touch alone. She feels the delicate symmetry of a leaf, the smooth skin of a silver birch and the rough, shaggy bark of a pine. In spring she touches branches for a bud, the first sign of Nature awakening after her winter sleep. Sometimes she is lucky enough to feel the happy quiver of a bird singing in a small tree. Still, her heart sometimes cries out to see. If touch gives so much pleasure, she thinks, sight must reveal far more beauty. The essay is written in a thoughtful, admiring and celebratory tone. Phrases such as smooth skin and rough, shaggy bark describe texture.
She would divide her three days into three parts. On the first day she would see the people whose kindness and companionship have made her life worth living. She calls the eye the window of the soul. She cannot see into a friend's heart through the eye, but only feels the outline of a face with her fingertips. She can detect laughter, sorrow and other obvious emotions that way, and she knows friends from the feel of their faces.
On the second day she would rise at dawn and watch the thrilling miracle of night turning into day, and the magnificent panorama of light with which the sun awakens the sleeping earth. She would then take a hasty glimpse of the world past and present and go to museums, to see the pageant of man's progress, with animals and races of people in their native places and the gigantic remains of dinosaurs and mastodons. She calls the earth sleeping to show that she imagines the dawn waking the world. The use of should again and again shows that these are wishes, not facts.
On the third morning she would greet the dawn again and spend the day among the places where people go about their daily lives. The city is her destination. She would stand at a busy corner just looking at people, to understand something of their lives. She would be happy seeing smiles, proud seeing serious determination and compassionate seeing suffering. At midnight permanent night would close in on her again. She says she would not have seen all she wanted, and only when darkness returned would she realise how much was left unseen.
She gives one hint to those who can see: use your eyes as if tomorrow you would be struck blind. The same applies to the other senses. Listen to voices, birdsong and music as if you would be struck deaf tomorrow, touch each object as if your touch would fail, and smell flowers and taste each morsel as if you could never smell or taste again. She asks us to make the most of every sense and glory in all the facets of beauty that Nature gives us. Of all the senses, she is sure that sight must be the most delightful. So touch makes up for some of her loss, but sight, she feels, is the most wonderful sense, and her choices of days show that she values people, nature, knowledge and understanding human life.
In the true or false exercise, the true statements are that she would spend the first day with people whose kind-heartedness enriched her life, that she knows she could not see everything in three days, that she advises people to appreciate every moment as if they might lose their senses, and that on the third day she wants to observe people in daily life. The false ones are that she mainly longs to hear, that she would explore the city only to see suffering, and that touch alone gives the greatest joy to everyone. Sensory words describe how we see, hear, smell, taste or feel. From the text, smooth, rough, shaggy and delicate are touch words, and perfume is a smell word.
A modal verb is an auxiliary verb that comes before the main verb and tells us about necessity, possibility, permission or ability. Common ones are can, could, may, might, shall, should, will, would, must and ought to. In I should divide the period, should is the modal and divide is the main verb. In the exercise, can shows ability or possibility, might shows possibility, must shows necessity, ought to shows advice or duty, and would shows a polite wish. In the situations: May I leave early today? I must finish this report by tomorrow. You ought to consider the pros and cons. It might rain later. Could you pass the salt, please? You should or ought to apologise. We can go to any park. In the listening conversation, Anuj meets a new classmate, Tara, who reads Braille. At first he thinks Digital India is only about computer literacy, but his mother explains that it also includes people with disabilities through assistive technology such as screen readers and voice-enabled smartphones, which let them use digital services independently and find more jobs. She ends by saying that inclusion needs the right mindset, not only the right tools. Use these points to choose the four true statements from the list.

why.en: Must shows that something has to be done.

text.en: Write the sentence.

why.en: You must finish your homework before dinner.

prompt.en: Explain what Helen Keller would do in her three days and what she advises.

requiredIdeas.en: Day one with friends, day two dawn and museums, day three the city and people.
She knows she could not see everything.
She advises using every sense as if it might fail tomorrow.
She believes sight is the most delightful sense.

commonMisconceptions.en: She would travel to many countries.
She says touch is the best sense for everyone.

points.en: Helen Keller imagines three days of sight, spent on friends, the world and its history, and people in a city.
Touch gives her pleasure, but she feels sight must be the most delightful sense.
She advises us to use all our senses as if we might lose them tomorrow.
Modal verbs such as should, can, must and might come before the main verb.
Sensory words describe sight, sound, smell, taste and touch.
